commands.name: docker
commands.summary: Build, run, and manage Linux containers and container images.
commands.risk_reason: Containers run as root by default; misconfigured mounts can expose the host filesystem.
cautions: Anyone who can run docker commands is effectively root on the host (the docker group is root-equivalent).
Mounting /var/run/docker.sock or / into a container hands that container control of the host.
Pin image tags or digests instead of :latest, and avoid running containers as root.
commands.explanation: docker manages the full container lifecycle. The daemon runs as root — use rootless Docker or podman for better security in production. Containers share the host kernel, so namespace escapes are a real risk on unpatched kernels.

examples.desc: List all containers with name, status, and ports in a clean table
Follow last 100 lines of container output
Open an interactive shell inside a running container

commands.pro_tip: Use `docker system prune -af` to remove all unused images, containers, and volumes — reclaims gigabytes on busy CI servers.

commands.name: docker ps
commands.risk_reason: Read-only listing.
commands.explanation: docker ps lists containers with their ID, image, command, status, and ports. The -a flag includes stopped containers. Combined with format strings, it produces machine-parseable output for automation.

examples.cmd: docker ps -q -f status=exited | xargs docker rm

commands.pro_tip: Use `docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'` to get container names for scripting — far cleaner than parsing default tabular output with awk.

commands.name: docker logs
commands.summary: Fetch and stream logs from a Docker container.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only log access.
commands.explanation: docker logs retrieves the stdout/stderr output of a container. The -f flag follows live output, --since filters by time, and --tail limits lines. For containers using json-file or local log drivers; doesn't work with syslog/journald drivers.

flags.desc: Number of lines to show from end
Show logs since timestamp or duration

examples.desc: Follow last 100 lines of container logs

commands.pro_tip: Use `docker logs --since $(date -d '1 hour ago' -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)` to get exactly one hour of logs aligned to UTC — useful for incident correlation.

commands.name: docker exec
commands.summary: Execute commands inside a running Docker container.
commands.risk_reason: Can modify container state; production containers should be treated as immutable.
cautions: Changes made inside a running container are lost on restart and are not tracked in Git.
In production, exec bypasses your deployment pipeline’s audit trail — prefer logs/metrics or a dedicated debug container.
Secrets passed with -e are visible in `docker inspect` and the process list.
commands.explanation: docker exec runs commands in running containers. The -it flags attach an interactive terminal. Used for debugging — checking configs, inspecting the filesystem, testing connectivity — without rebuilding the image.

examples.cmd: docker exec mycontainer env | grep DB

commands.pro_tip: If bash isn't available, try `docker exec -it container sh` — Alpine-based images don't include bash. Also try `docker exec -it container /bin/ash`.

commands.name: docker build
commands.summary: Build a Docker image from a Dockerfile.
commands.risk_reason: Network access during build; large images consume disk space.
commands.explanation: docker build creates images from a Dockerfile. The -t flag tags the image. Build context (the path argument) is sent to the Docker daemon — use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files and speed up builds.

flags.desc: Name and optionally tag the image

examples.desc: Build and tag image from current directory

commands.pro_tip: Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing — COPY requirements.txt and RUN pip install before COPY . . — to maximize cache layer reuse and reduce build times.

commands.name: podman
commands.summary: Daemonless container runtime compatible with Docker CLI.
commands.risk_reason: Rootless by default; some Docker behaviors differ.
cautions: Rootless mode limits privileges, but --privileged or mounting host paths still gives broad access.
Docker-compatible flags can behave differently (networking, volume ownership, systemd integration) — test before production use.
commands.explanation: Podman is a daemonless container engine that's fully OCI-compatible and largely drop-in compatible with Docker commands. It runs rootless by default (more secure), supports pods natively (like Kubernetes pods), and generates Kubernetes YAML from running containers.

examples.desc: List all containers (same syntax as docker ps)
Generate Kubernetes YAML from running container
Show disk usage by containers, images, volumes

commands.pro_tip: Use `podman generate kube container_name` to convert a working local container to Kubernetes YAML — faster than writing manifests from scratch when prototyping.

commands.name: skopeo
commands.summary: Inspect, copy, and sync container images without a runtime.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only inspection; copy operations require write access.
commands.explanation: skopeo operates on container images in registries without needing a container runtime or root. It inspects images (tags, layers, config), copies images between registries, and syncs registry contents. Essential for registry migrations and air-gapped environments.

examples.desc: Inspect nginx image metadata without pulling
List all available tags for an image
Copy image to local OCI directory

commands.pro_tip: Use `skopeo list-tags` in CI to check if a specific image tag exists before pulling — prevents misleading 'image not found' errors mid-pipeline.

commands.name: docker-compose
commands.risk_reason: `down -v` deletes volumes; the wrong project/directory affects the wrong stack.
cautions: `down -v` or `rm -v` deletes named volumes — data loss.
Check the directory and project name (-p); the same service names exist in many stacks.
`up` recreates containers when images or config changed.
commands.explanation: Compose v1 binary; use `docker compose` (v2) today. Reads docker-compose.yml.

safer.why: Validate and view the resolved config

commands.name: docker compose
commands.risk_reason: `down -v` deletes volumes; the wrong project/directory affects the wrong stack.
cautions: Volumes survive `down` but not `down -v`.
Verify the project (docker compose ls) before destructive commands.
`up` recreates containers when config/image changed — expect a brief outage.
commands.explanation: Compose v2 plugin: manages the services in compose.yaml.

commands.name: docker run
commands.risk_reason: Containers can mount host paths, use host networking or run privileged.
cautions: --privileged, -v /:/host and -v /var/run/docker.sock grant host-level control.
Pin image tags/digests; avoid :latest.
Don’t pass secrets with -e — use secrets or env files with strict permissions.
Run as non-root (--user) and drop capabilities (--cap-drop ALL).
commands.explanation: Creates and starts a container from an image.

flags.caution: Mounting / or the Docker socket gives host control.

commands.name: docker rm
commands.risk_reason: Deletes containers and, with -v, their anonymous volumes.
cautions: -v deletes anonymous volumes (often databases).
`docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq)` removes every container on the host.
commands.explanation: Removes stopped containers; -f kills running ones.

commands.name: docker rmi
commands.risk_reason: Removes images; running containers may need them to restart.
cautions: Images referenced by stopped containers stop those containers from being recreated.
commands.explanation: Deletes local images. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: docker stop
commands.risk_reason: Stops services; sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after the timeout.
cautions: `docker stop $(docker ps -q)` stops every container on the host.
Databases may need a longer -t to flush data.
commands.explanation: Gracefully stops containers; default timeout 10 s.

commands.name: docker system prune
commands.risk_reason: Deletes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images; with -a --volumes also unused images and volumes.
cautions: "Unused" means not referenced by a running container — stopped databases’ volumes can be deleted with --volumes.
-f skips the confirmation prompt.
commands.explanation: Cleans up disk space used by Docker. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: docker volume
commands.risk_reason: `rm`/`prune` permanently delete data.
cautions: Volume data is not backed up by default.
prune deletes volumes not currently used by a container — including those of stopped databases.
commands.explanation: Create, list and remove volumes. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: docker network
commands.risk_reason: Removing/disconnecting networks breaks container connectivity.
cautions: Removing a network used by services breaks them.
commands.explanation: Create, inspect and remove networks. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: docker pull
commands.risk_reason: Downloads images from a registry — untrusted images may be malicious.
cautions: Only pull from trusted registries; verify digests/signatures.
Avoid :latest in production.
commands.explanation: Fetches an image. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: docker push
commands.risk_reason: Publishes images; may expose code or secrets baked into layers.
cautions: Images can contain secrets in layers — scan before pushing.
Pushing to the wrong registry or tag (e.g. overwriting :prod) affects deployments.
commands.explanation: Pushes an image to a registry. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: docker inspect
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; output may include secrets (env vars).
cautions: Environment variables (passwords, tokens) are visible — don’t paste output into tickets.
commands.explanation: Returns JSON details of containers, images, networks and volumes.

commands.name: docker stats
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Streams CPU, memory, network and I/O per container.

commands.name: docker cp
commands.risk_reason: Overwrites files inside containers/host.
cautions: Copying into running containers changes state outside your deployment pipeline.
commands.explanation: Copies between a container and the host.

commands.name: docker login
commands.risk_reason: Stores credentials in ~/.docker/config.json.
cautions: Use --password-stdin; avoid -p on the command line.
Credentials stored in config.json are base64 only — use a credential helper.
commands.explanation: Saves registry credentials. See the flags and examples below, and run `man docker` for the full reference.

commands.name: buildah
commands.summary: Build OCI images without a daemon
commands.risk_reason: Builds run commands as the invoking user; rootless recommended.
cautions: Builds execute arbitrary RUN steps — only build trusted Dockerfiles.
commands.explanation: Daemonless image builder from Red Hat. See the flags and examples below, and run `man buildah` for the full reference.

commands.name: ctr
commands.risk_reason: Operates below Kubernetes; can delete containers/images used by the kubelet.
cautions: Changes made with ctr are invisible to Kubernetes and can leave nodes inconsistent.
commands.explanation: Low-level client for containerd. See the flags and examples below, and run `man ctr` for the full reference.

commands.name: nerdctl
commands.risk_reason: Mirrors Docker risks.
cautions: Same risks as docker run --privileged and host mounts.
commands.explanation: Docker-like CLI for containerd. See the flags and examples below, and run `man nerdctl` for the full reference.

commands.name: trivy
commands.risk_reason: Read-only scan; downloads vulnerability DBs.
cautions: Findings need triage — a clean scan is not a guarantee.
commands.explanation: Scans images, filesystems and IaC for CVEs and misconfigurations.

commands.name: hadolint
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Checks Dockerfiles for best practices. See the flags and examples below, and run `man hadolint` for the full reference.

commands.name: dive
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: TUI showing image layers and wasted space.

commands.name: lxc
commands.risk_reason: Manages system containers with privileged options.
cautions: Privileged containers and device passthrough weaken isolation.
commands.explanation: lxc commands manage LXD instances. See the flags and examples below, and run `man lxc` for the full reference.
